title: B.C.'s new premier outlines 3 immediate priorities after first cabinet meeting
summary: B.C. Premier Lorne Doerkson says he's taking immediate action on three top priorities after his first cabinet meeting. They include posting a notice of intent for a design of a bridge option to…

blocks.text: British Columbia

B.C. Premier Lorne Doerkson says he's taking immediate action on three top priorities after his first cabinet meeting. They include posting a notice of intent for a design of a bridge option to replace the George Massey Tunnel, taking SOGI 123 materials off government websites, and starting a return-to-office plan for the B.C. Public Service.
Lorne Doerkson's top 3 to-dos: George Massey replacement, removing SOGI materials, return-to-office
B.C. Premier Lorne Doerkson has announced he's taking immediate action on three top priorities after his first cabinet meeting.
Doerkson listed his first priority as posting a notice of intent for a design of a bridge option to replace the George Massey Tunnel between Richmond and Delta.
He said at a news conference Wednesday afternoon the notice would be posted later in the day and will ask the current contractor to do the work.
He said cabinet would review the numbers before making a final decision to ensure the project is the most cost-effective.
"Our responsibility is to ensure taxpayers get the best value for their money," Doerkson said.
He said British Columbians want access over the river, and he wants the space to understand the project.
"I am, obviously, very big on 'bridge' right now, but I do want to understand a few things just before that final decision happens, and I hope that to happen before Christmas."
The previous B.C. NDP government had planned to replace the tunnel, rather than build a bridge.

blocks.text: Secondly, Doerkson said SOGI 123 materials will be taken off government websites "as of today."

SOGI (which stands for sexual orientation and gender identity) 123 has been a resource teachers and educators can turn to to make schools safer and more inclusive for students of all gender identities and orientations, according to its website.
Doerkson said the Ministry of Education will work with school districts to take SOGI 123 materials out of schools.
"We are starting that work right now."
He said parents should have a say in how and when "sensitive topics" are introduced in schools.
"We want our schools to be safe and welcoming places, of course, for every student, with a strong focus on reading, writing, arithmetic and on teaching kids to think for themselves," Doerkson said.

blocks.text: He said he wants to "better understand how our schools were not safe prior to SOGI" and "how we will make sure that our student body is safe."
He added: "SOGI, of course, has been conflated with so much now — I'm not certain that I've even been able to get a good explanation from ministry staff or from teachers, frankly, on this topic."
Doerkson responded to a reporter's question on what would happen if teachers continue to use the SOGI resource.
"We've asked for it to be removed from the rooms, so it's not just that they'll get pushback from parents, but they'll get pushback from me as well."
Return-to-office planned for public servants
Doerkson's third priority is for B.C. Public Service workers to return to the office in a phased plan.
Those who can work from the office "will be back at it, five days a week," Doerkson said.
He said he's written to the head of the public service to start planning for the return-to-office policy.
He said thousands of public servants, such as nurses, teachers, correctional workers and those providing frontline services, have never had the choice to work remotely.
"I think it's reasonable to ask for people in our offices to do the same," Doerkson said, adding people collaborate better in the same room.
